title: Diversity of stripped-envelope supernova light curves from interaction with binary-driven circumstellar material
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures, 1 table. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics (A&A)
summary: A growing number of core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe) exhibit diverse light-curve morphologies that indicate strong interaction with dense, pre-existing circumstellar material (CSM). Understanding the physical origin of such CSM is essential for exploring the late-stage evolution of SN progenitors. Non-conservative mass transfer during binary interactions provides a promising channel for producing dense CSM before core collapse. Using the stellar evolution code MESA, we simulate post-common-envelope binaries that give rise to ultra-stripped progenitors and self-consistently construct the CSM from mass loss during binary evolution. We further analytically predict the resulting bolometric and radio light curves by following the shock dynamics of SN ejecta interacting with the CSM. We find that surface-radius variations in the ultra-stripped progenitors trigger multiple episodes of mass transfer and produce diverse CSM density profiles, including detached shells and multi-peaked structures. Interaction with such CSM gives rise to non-monotonic, multi-peaked optical and radio light curves that qualitatively resemble features observed in some stripped-envelope SNe. Long-term multi-wavelength monitoring of stripped-envelope SN candidates, particularly at late times, will be crucial for probing structured CSM and constraining the mass-loss history of stripped progenitors. Our results suggest that SN-CSM interaction in binaries hosting ultra-stripped progenitors provides a possible channel for producing diverse light-curve morphologies, highlighting a potential connection between the pre-SN evolution of massive binary stars and the diversity of their explosive transients.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how binary interactions producing ultra-stripped supernova progenitors can generate diverse circumstellar material (CSM) structures, leading to multi-peaked optical and radio light curves that explain observed morphologies in stripped-envelope supernovae.
AI.motivation: Many core-collapse supernovae show diverse light-curve morphologies indicating strong interaction with dense pre-existing CSM, but the physical origin of such CSM is not well understood. Understanding this connection is essential for probing the late-stage evolution of SN progenitors.
AI.method: The authors use the stellar evolution code MESA to simulate post-common-envelope binaries that produce ultra-stripped progenitors, self-consistently constructing CSM from binary mass loss. They analytically predict bolometric and radio light curves by modeling the shock dynamics of SN ejecta interacting with the CSM.
AI.result: Surface-radius variations in ultra-stripped progenitors trigger multiple episodes of mass transfer, producing diverse CSM density profiles including detached shells and multi-peaked structures. The resulting SN-CSM interaction yields non-monotonic, multi-peaked optical and radio light curves that qualitatively resemble observed stripped-envelope SNe features.
AI.conclusion: SN-CSM interaction in binaries hosting ultra-stripped progenitors provides a viable channel for diverse light-curve morphologies. Long-term multi-wavelength monitoring, especially at late times, is crucial for probing structured CSM and constraining mass-loss histories of stripped progenitors, highlighting a link between pre-SN binary evolution and transient diversity.

title: Path to Black Hole Astrometric Microlensing from 10-Year KMTNet Database
summary: I present a Fisher analysis of the astrometric signature of black holes (BHs) that may lie in the 10-year KMTNet microlensing database, motivated by the recent success of the pilot study by Segev et al. (2026), which reduced the scatter at $I=18$ to $σ\sim 10\,$mas. Seeing-limited ground-based observations still suffer from a great deal of systematics, but under the assumption that these systematics can be controlled, I find that with this nominal precision, the Einstein radius can be measured with errors $σ(θ_{\rm E})\sim 0.5\,$mas in the most intensively monitored fields ($\sim 12\,$deg$^2$), and hence to twice that value in an additional $\sim 28\,$deg$^2$ area. This precision hardly depends on whether the peak of the event is during the observing season or not, as long as the impact parameter is within the broad range that is accessible to photometric recognition of the event, i.e., $u_0\lesssim 1.5$. However, longer events do have somewhat better precision. The analysis presented here ignores blending, but this is a good first approximation for most sources $I\lesssim 18$, which lie near or on the giant branch. I outline a practical program, combining photometric and astrometric searches, aimed at identifying isolated BHs in the KMTNet database and measuring their masses and distances.

AI.tldr: A Fisher analysis of the astrometric microlensing signature of black holes in the 10-year KMTNet database shows that with ~10 mas precision (as achieved in a recent pilot study), the Einstein radius can be measured with errors of ~0.5 mas in the most intensively monitored fields (~12 deg²), with precision largely insensitive to event timing or impact parameter, though longer events in is benefit. A practical program combining photometric and astrometric searches is outlined to identify isolated black holes and measure their masses and distances.
AI.motivation: To assess the feasibility of detecting and characterizing isolated black holes via astrometric microlensing using the 10-year KMTNet database, motivated by recent improvements in astrometric precision to ~10 mas at I=18.
AI.method: Fisher analysis of the astrometric signature of black hole microlensing events, assuming systematic errors can be controlled to the nominal ~10 mas precision achieved in a pilot study, and ignoring blending (a good approximation for sources with I≲18 near or on the giant branch).
AI.result: The Einstein radius can be measured with σ(θ_E)~0.5 mas in the ~12 deg² of most intensively monitored fields, and ~1 mas (twice that) in an additional ~28 deg². Precision is largely independent of whether the peak occurs in-season or not, provided u_0≲1.5, though longer events yield somewhat better precision.
AI.conclusion: With controlled systematics, ground-based astrometric microlensing from KMTNet can measure black hole Einstein radii precisely enough to support a practical program combining photometric and astrometric searches to identify isolated black holes and measure their masses and distances.

title: Numerical modelling of recombination-driven stellar winds
summary: Low-temperature stars have a significant population of neutral hydrogen increasing with height in their atmospheres. This suggests eventual recombination as we move away from their deep photospheric layers. Recombination can potentially drive stellar winds, particularly in cool and evolved stars. We aim to verify the possibility of stellar winds driven by recombination. We also aim to constitute an initial model for this type wind driving. We examine the possibility of recombination-driven outflows across the HR diagram by comparing the gravitational potential energy per atom to the hydrogen ionization energy. Then we start from a simple analytical model with the addition of an extra heating term to the gas in the Parker wind model. We model the heating term, analogous to the heat released by recombination, and examine how it can drive an outflow. We implement the model in the code CASTRO and check the hydrodynamic stability of the solution. The added heating drives a steady transonic outflow in our models, when tested with the parameters of an AGB star. The heating function affects the solution and the location of the sonic point depends on the location of the heating function itself. Even though the derived hydrodynamic equations are independent of the density, we determine the processes that set the mass-loss rate. By comparing the heating from collisional recombination and cooling due to radiative recombination, we show that relatively high densities are required to release the recombination energy as heat, implying mass-loss rates of the order of 0.1 solar mass per year. Our comparison of energies across the HR diagram suggests a possibility of recombination-driven winds in evolved red giants and AGB stars. The main deciding factor for wind launching is the radial distribution of heat released by recombination in a star's atmosphere. This can in turn affect the mass-loss rate.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether stellar winds can be driven by hydrogen recombination in cool, evolved stars. Using an analytical Parker wind model enhanced with an extra heating term (analogous to recombination heat release) and verified in the CASTRO hydrodynamic code, the authors find that recombination can indeed drive steady transonic outflows. They determine that relatively high densities are required to release recombination energy as heat, implying mass-loss rates on the order of 0.1 solar masses per year for evolved red giants and AGB stars.
AI.motivation: Low-temperature stars show increasing neutral hydrogen populations with atmospheric height, suggesting recombination occurs away from deep photospheric layers. Since recombination can potentially release energy to drive outflows, the authors aim to verify whether recombination-driven stellar winds are physically possible and to establish an initial model for this wind-driving mechanism across the HR diagram.
AI.method: The authors compare gravitational potential energy per atom to hydrogen ionization energy across the HR diagram to assess the possibility of recombination-driven winds. They construct a simple analytical model by adding an extra heating term to the Parker wind model, analogous to heat released by recombination. The model is implemented in the CASTRO hydrodynamic code to check the stability of the solution, and they compare collisional recombination heating versus radiative recombination cooling to constrain densities and mass-loss rates.
AI.result: The added heating drives a steady transonic outflow in their models when tested with AGB star parameters. The heating function location determines the sonic point position. While the derived hydrodynamic equations are density-independent, the authors identify the processes that set the mass-loss rate: relatively high densities are required to release recombination energy as heat, implying mass-loss rates of about 0.1 solar masses per year. Energy comparisons across the HR diagram suggest recombination-driven winds are possible in evolved red giants and AGB stars.
AI.conclusion: Recombination-driven winds are a viable mechanism for outflows in evolved red giants and AGB stars. The key factor determining wind launching is the radial distribution of recombination heat released in the stellar atmosphere, which in turn controls the mass-loss rate.
